title: Microbiome Balance
description: Interactive cartoon model of a gut bacterial community with 24 made-up species in five groups. Learners give an antibiotic course or switch between a fiber-rich and a low-fiber diet and watch the diversity index, community makeup, and species count change. Antibiotics knock diversity down and let opportunists bloom; most of the community regrows, but rare species that hit zero are lost, so recovery is partial and differs between simulated people.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Predict how an antibiotic course changes the diversity and makeup of a gut bacterial community, including a temporary bloom of opportunist bacteria.
Explain why recovery after antibiotics is often partial and differs between people.
Describe how a low-fiber diet shifts community makeup and why the change can reverse when fiber returns if no species are lost.
prerequisites: Bacteria as living cells that grow and compete for food and space
The colon as the part of the gut where most bacteria live
Reading a simple line chart and a stacked bar chart
keyQuestions: What happens to gut diversity during and after an antibiotic course?
Why can opportunist bacteria bloom when commensals are knocked down?
Why doesn't every species come back after antibiotics?
Why do two people respond differently to the same antibiotic?
misconceptions: One course of antibiotics ruins the microbiome forever.
The gut microbiome always returns exactly to where it started.
All bacteria are harmful, so fewer bacteria is better.
Everyone responds to antibiotics in the same way.
